title: Glasshouse and Wardrobe
premise: After his mother's funeral, Dominic Okonkwo returns to the family glasshouse to catalog her belongings and finds a letter requesting that he study with Adaora Eze, the last fluent speaker of Ọ̀nà, a dying language his mother secretly spoke. As lessons deepen, Dominic uncovers his mother's hidden life—her forbidden love for a woman, her exile from her own tongue—and realizes the language was silenced along with everything else she loved. When Adaora's health fails and developers threaten the community garden where they meet, Dominic must choose between the polished heir he performs and the person his mother never got to be. The novel ends with Dominic delivering his mother's eulogy, finally, in Ọ̀nà—at her reopened grave-side gathering months later—speaking aloud both her name and his own truth as the last student of a last speaker.
about_author: Coral Sandoval is the pen name of a Nigerian-British writer who grew up between Lagos and Manchester, translating between parents who shared no common grief. Their work explores inheritance, silence, and the languages families lose on purpose.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV at the funeral reception, performing flawless condolences while feeling nothing land. Establishes the perfected social mask and the numbness beneath it. Emotional beat: hollow competence masking grief.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Stranger
chapters.summary: Dominic begins cataloging his mother Ngozi's possessions in the family home, finding nothing personal—no letters, no photographs of her youth. POV: Dominic. Beat: the eerie blankness of a parent's curated silence.

chapters.title: The Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Dominic discovers the neglected Victorian glasshouse behind the house, where his mother supposedly 'kept plants.' Inside: dead orchids and one living, unlabeled vine. Beat: first crack in the official story.

chapters.title: A Letter in an Unknown Hand
chapters.summary: Among seed catalogs, Dominic finds a letter from an 'A. Eze' asking Ngozi to send 'the boy' for lessons. The handwriting is warm; the request is urgent. Beat: intrigue displacing numbness.

chapters.title: Adaora
chapters.summary: Dominic tracks down Adaora Eze, ninety-one, sharp-tongued, living above a shuttered bakery. She mistakes him for his mother at first—and weeps. Beat: grief reflected back by a stranger.

chapters.title: First Lesson
chapters.summary: Reluctantly, Dominic agrees to one lesson. Adaora teaches greetings in Ọ̀nà, a language he's never heard. His mouth fails around the tones. Beat: humiliation that feels strangely like relief.

chapters.title: What the Family Knew
chapters.summary: Dominic's father Charles dismisses the lessons as sentimentality; Aunt Bisi warns him to leave Adaora alone. Flashback fragments: Ngozi never speaking Igbo or anything else at home. Beat: the machinery of enforced forgetting.

chapters.title: The Word for Refuse
chapters.summary: Adaora teaches the word for 'refuse/no'—and Dominic uses it for the first time in his life, declining a business dinner. Small act, seismic feeling. Beat: language as permission.

chapters.title: Ngozi's Notebook
chapters.summary: In the glasshouse, hidden in a false pot bottom, Dominic finds his mother's old notebook: Ọ̀nà vocabulary, pressed flowers, and a woman's name—Ruth—written and scratched out repeatedly. Beat: the secret takes shape.

chapters.title: Ruth
chapters.summary: Dominic finds Ruth Adeyemi, now in her eighties, running a community garden across town. Ruth confirms she and Ngozi loved each other in the 1970s, before Ngozi chose respectability. Beat: the mother becomes a whole person.

chapters.title: Two Women, One Silence
chapters.summary: Ruth recounts how Ngozi's family discovered them; how Ngozi married Charles within a year and stopped speaking Ọ̀nà—the language she'd learned in Ruth's household—to erase the evidence of that life. Beat: heartbreak of chosen erasure.

chapters.title: The Heir Apparent
chapters.summary: Charles pressures Dominic to sell the house and glasshouse to developers; the family firm needs capital. Dominic, ever obedient, nearly signs. Beat: duty tightening its grip.

chapters.title: Tones
chapters.summary: Lesson montage: Adaora's health wobbles but her teaching intensifies. Dominic learns that Ọ̀nà has no word for 'heir'—only 'the one who carries.' Beat: identity reframed through vocabulary.

chapters.title: The Garden Party
chapters.summary: At a family gala, Dominic catches himself answering a cousin in Ọ̀nà under his breath. A relative notices something is different about him. Beat: the mask slipping in public.

chapters.title: Adaora's Story
chapters.summary: Adaora tells her own history: missionary schools, punished tongues, a generation taught to be ashamed. She is the last speaker because everyone else was made to stop. Beat: political weight behind the personal.

chapters.title: Recording
chapters.summary: Dominic begins recording lessons on his phone, then properly, with a microphone. Adaora jokes about becoming a museum; the joke lands wrong. Beat: urgency sharpening into mortality.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: A university linguist contacts Dominic after hearing rumors, offering to help document Ọ̀nà—but wants control of the materials and Adaora's cooperation on their terms. Beat: rescue that smells like capture.

chapters.title: Charles's Ultimatum
chapters.summary: Charles gives Dominic a deadline: sign the sale papers or step out of the family firm. He invokes Ngozi's memory as leverage. Beat: love against duty, externalized.

chapters.title: The Vine Blooms
chapters.summary: The unlabeled vine in the glasshouse flowers—Ruth identifies it as a cutting from her own garden, planted the year Ngozi married. Proof of what survived. Beat: quiet devastation and hope.

chapters.title: Learning to Say Mother
chapters.summary: Adaora teaches the word for 'mother'; Dominic cannot say it without breaking. First full crying scene. Beat: grief finally given grammar.

chapters.title: Bisi's Confession
chapters.summary: Aunt Bisi admits she knew about Ruth—that she was the one who told Ngozi's father, believing it would save her. Her guilt has calcified into piety. Beat: complicity revealed, forgiveness withheld.

chapters.title: The Hospital
chapters.summary: Adaora is hospitalized after a fall. Lessons move to her ward, whispered between beeping machines. Dominic reads her the notebook. Beat: time visibly running out.

chapters.title: What Ngozi Wrote Last
chapters.summary: The notebook's final pages, in failing handwriting, are a letter to Dominic: an apology for the silence, and a plea that he learn 'so someone will know I existed entirely.' Beat: the mother speaks at last, posthumously.

chapters.title: Signing Day
chapters.summary: Dominic sits before the sale contract, pen in hand, and walks out without signing. He calls the university instead—but on his own terms. Beat: the refusal that changes everything.

chapters.title: Disowned, Lighter
chapters.summary: Charles cuts Dominic off financially and socially. Stripped of the firm, the flat, the role, Dominic moves temporarily into the glasshouse cottage. Beat: loss experienced as liberation.

chapters.title: Partnership with Ruth
chapters.summary: Dominic and Ruth formally partner: the garden will host classes, recordings, and eventually an archive. Old love and new purpose braid together. Beat: community forming where family failed.

chapters.title: The Developers Return
chapters.summary: The developer files anyway, claiming the glasshouse land. Legal threat arrives with a court date. Beat: rising external stakes.

chapters.title: Teaching Others
chapters.summary: Three neighbors—a teenager, a retired nurse, a Somali refugee—join lessons. Dominic, barely intermediate, teaches alongside Adaora. Beat: the last speaker becomes the first teacher of many.

chapters.title: Adaora's Request
chapters.summary: Adaora asks Dominic for a promise: when she dies, he must speak at her service in Ọ̀nà—not English. 'A language dies politely otherwise,' she says. Beat: the weight of succession.

chapters.title: The Court Hearing
chapters.summary: Dominic testifies about the glasshouse's heritage value, speaking publicly, unpolished, unmasked—for the first time in his life. Ruling deferred. Beat: public vulnerability as climax rehearsal.

chapters.title: Night Conversation
chapters.summary: Adaora, discharged, tells Dominic she doesn't fear dying—only being misquoted. They record her life story over three nights. Beat: intimacy, legacy, tenderness.

chapters.title: Charles at the Door
chapters.summary: Charles appears at the glasshouse, unannounced, having read Ngozi's letter (Bisi gave it to him). He says nothing kind, but he doesn't condemn. Ambiguous thaw. Beat: the possibility of imperfect reconciliation.

chapters.title: The Ruling
chapters.summary: The court grants preservation status to the glasshouse and garden, citing cultural significance. The developer withdraws. Beat: victory, hard-won and slightly anticlimactic—correctly so.

chapters.title: Adaora's Decline
chapters.summary: Adaora stops leaving her bed. Lessons continue there; she corrects Dominic's tones with closing eyes. She tells him he's ready. He isn't. Beat: approaching climax, dread and gratitude entwined.

chapters.title: The Last Full Lesson
chapters.summary: Adaora teaches the funeral rites vocabulary—the words for goodbye, for 'go well,' for 'we will carry you.' She makes him repeat each until perfect. Beat: transmission complete; the torch passed.

chapters.title: Go Well
chapters.summary: Adaora dies peacefully with Dominic holding her hand, saying the going-well blessing over her in Ọ̀nà as she once said it over students. Beat: death met with fluency, not helplessness.

chapters.title: Two Eulogies
chapters.summary: At Adaora's service, Dominic delivers the eulogy entirely in Ọ̀nà, voice steady, tears falling. Half the congregation understands nothing; everyone understands everything. Beat: emotional climax.

chapters.title: Reburial of Words
chapters.summary: Months later, the family holds a delayed memorial for Ngozi at the garden. Dominic delivers the eulogy he couldn't give at the funeral—in Ọ̀nà, naming Ruth, naming the truth. Charles attends. Says nothing. Stays. Beat: resolution of the silence.

chapters.title: The Archive Opens
chapters.summary: The Ọ̀nà archive opens in the restored glasshouse: recordings, the notebook, Adaora's story. Dominic is listed not as heir but as 'carrier of the language.' Beat: identity remade.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Final chapter: Dominic greets a new student—a child from the neighborhood—with the greeting Adaora first taught him. The vine blooms again. He answers his own reflection's smile with a real one. Beat: belonging achieved; the language lives.
